name: Asbuk
title: Father of Nehemiah, the ruler over half of the Beth-zur district
summary: Asbuk is known exclusively from the book of Nehemiah, where he is identified as the father of a man named Nehemiah – another person than the main character of the book, Nehemiah son of Hakalja. The son Nehemiah, son of Asbuk, served as governor over half of the district of Beth-Shur and participated in the major joint project to rebuild Jerusalem's wall after returning from the Babylonian exile. According to Neh 3:16, he was responsible for a section of the wall that extended to a point opposite the tombs of David, the raised pool, and the Fortress of Zion. Asbuk is attributed no actions of his own in the text, but the mention of his son in a prominent leadership role suggests that the family had local influence in the Judean highlands under Persian rule. Beth-Shur was a strategically important fortified city, and the family's connection to it underscores their position within the administrative structure of the province of Yehud.
roles: father of one of the wall builders

keyEvents.title: Son Nehemiah participates in rebuilding Jerusalem's wall
keyEvents.description: Nehemiah, son of Asbuk and ruler over half of the Beth-zur district, worked on repairing a section of Jerusalem's wall. His section extended to a point opposite the tombs of David, the artificial pool, and the Tower of the Furnace. This work was part of an extensive national restoration project led by Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah.

versions.summary: Asbuk is mentioned in the book of Nehemiah as the father of Nehemiah (not to be confused with the book's main character, Nehemiah son of Hacaliah). His son Nehemiah was the ruler over half of the Beth-zur district and participated in rebuilding Jerusalem's wall.
versions.title: Father of Nehemiah, ruler in Beth-zur
versions.reason: [minor] The title actually describes the son's role, not Asbuk's own. Asbuk himself is only known as the father of Nehemiah, who was a governor. It is more precise to say 'Father of Nehemiah, the governor in Beth-Sur' to clarify that it was the son who served as governor.; [major] Asbuk is not described as a 'leader' in the Bible. He is mentioned only as the father of Nehemiah (son of Asbuk). We know nothing about his own roles. 'Father' would be more appropriate, or alternatively the list could remain empty or contain a neutral description.; [minor] The second key event (the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall) with verses 1–16 is very broad and concerns the entire wall-building project, not specifically Asbuk. The third and fourth events overlap significantly with the first one. For someone mentioned in only one verse, this is an excessive number of events. It is recommended to reduce this to 1–2 events.; [minor] The description mentions 'near the tombs of David', but this is taken from Nehemiah 3:16, which refers to Nehemiah son of Asbuk. The verse actually mentions the tombs of David in connection with that section of the wall, but verses 17–18 concern the work of other people, not Asbuk's son.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but could be clarified somewhat. It is correct that a distinction is made between this Nehemiah and the book's main character, Nehemiah son of Hakalja.; [minor] The ID 'nehemja-ben-asbuk' is a reasonable identifier, but it should be verified that this ID is actually used consistently in the system.

footnotes.text: The name Asbuk (Hebrew: עַזְבּוּק, 'Azbûq) appears only once in the Bible, in Neh 3:16. Its etymology is debated; it may derive from the root עזב ('azav, 'to leave') with a suffix element, or possibly from a root related to strength. The rare name's single occurrence makes its interpretation uncertain.

Beth-zur (Hebrew: בֵּית צוּר) was a fortified city about 8 km north of Hebron. Archaeological excavations have revealed fortifications from the Persian period, confirming the city's importance as an administrative and military center after the exile.

During the Persian period, the province of Yehud (Judah) was divided into administrative districts called pelekh (פֶּלֶךְ). Nehemiah 3 mentions several 'half-districts,' indicating that the Persians organized the region into smaller units for efficient administration and taxation.

The tombs of David, mentioned in Neh 3:16, were a well-known landmark in ancient Jerusalem. According to biblical and Jewish tradition, these tombs were located on the southeastern hill, in what is called the City of David. Josephus confirms that the tombs were still known in the first century C.E.

Nehemiah 3 provides a remarkably detailed topographical description of Jerusalem's wall, naming the work leaders, their hometowns, and which section they worked on. The chapter serves as an important source for reconstructing the extent of Jerusalem in Persian times.

The term 'House of Heroes' (Hebrew: בֵּית הַגִּבֹּרִים, Bet ha-Gibborim) in Neh 3:16 likely refers to a military garrison or barracks housing elite soldiers. Some scholars connect it with David's 'heroes' (gibborim), known from 2 Sam 23.
